The city council deferred a second reading of ordinances implementing the codes, originally scheduled for August 17. Council instead instructed staff to conduct additional public outreach. The proposal was drafted after two public surveys and five public outreach forums, to an overall favorable view by residents. Survey results in the first reading found that 66 percent of residents supported the proposal, but some residents have voiced concerns. “Requiring all-electric cooking facilities is a big mistake, and is a deal-breaker,” claimed resident Bruce Joffe. “It does not significantly reduce CO2 emissions because most of the electricity that is generated comes from burning carbon. articles.text: Alameda County allows public pools to open After five months of closure, Alameda County swimming pools are now allowed to re-open under loosened shelter-in-place guidelines. The guidance came in a statement from Alameda County Public Health Department more than a week ago, on August 21. “[This] outdoor activity we are allowing to reopen is relatively low-risk,” Interim Health Officer Dr. Nicholas Moss said. This is the first guidance issued by Alameda County for the reopening of pools. The Piedmont Community Pool has remained closed due to COVID- 19, but has now been given the green-light to reopen. City staff is determining whether the conditions imposed by the order can be applied in a way that makes sense to reopen the pool. Recreation Department staff members had previously developed reopening frameworks based upon guidance from other health jurisdictions. The 56-year-old pool is showing its age and is leaking approximately 3,000 gallons of water each day. City Council has decided to place a measure on the November 3 ballot that aims to address these problems. Measure UU, a $19.5 million bond, would replace the three existing pools with two pools. The measure is supported by Mayor Bob McBain, councilmember Betsy Andersen, Recreation Chair Steven Roland, Board of Education member Sarah Pearson, and retired Beach School Principal Nancy McHugh. The September 8 City Council agenda will include an update from city staff on the feasibility of reopening the pool in its current condition. Recreation Director Chelle Putzer, Finance Director Michael Szczech, and City Administrator Sara Lillevand are currently working on a report that will be presented publicly at the meeting.
articles.title: City Council to consider reopening pool

articles.text: Unhealthy air quality conditions shrouded Piedmont this week as a trio of wildfires continued to blaze around the Bay Area. The Bay Area Air Qualit y Management Dist r ict (BAAQMD) extended a “Spare the Air” alert for the Bay Area, including Piedmont, through Tuesday, September 1. This marked 15 consecutive days of Spare the Air alerts, a bleak record for the agency. When Spare the Air warnings are in effect, people are advised to limit their times outdoors, especially those who are sensitive to air conditions. Additionally, the use of fireplaces, wood stoves, pellet stoves, outdoor fire pits or other wood-burning devices is prohibited. Three fires caused by lightning strikes in mid-August are the cause of the unhealthy air quality. The SCU Lightning Complex, which has burned over 390,000 acres and has the largest footprint of the three blazes, is burning in rural Stanislaus and San Joaquin counties. It was 70 percent contained as of press time. Fires in Napa and Sonoma counties, the LNU Lightning Complex, have proven to be the deadliest and most destructive. Five people have died, and 1,288 structures have been destroyed. CalFire reports that over 3,300 structures are still threatened, even as the fire is now 69 percent contained. With a size of 85,218 acres, the CZU Lightning Complex, between San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties, is the smallest of the three fires is the least contained. Cal Fire said that it was only 43 percent contained as of yesterday. One person has died in this wildfire. articles.text: Alameda County falls under most restrictive “purple” tier During a press briefing on August 28, Gov. Gavin Newsom announced new guidelines for reopening the counties that have previously been on the state watch list. The watch list has been replaced with a new, four-tiered color-coded reopening system based on coronavirus prevalence and testing rates. The new model is officially named “The Blueprint for a Safer Economy,” and its primary focus is to determine what businesses can and cannot open. “COVID-19 will be with us for a long time and we need to adapt,” Newsom said. The new model went into effect this week on Monday, August 31. “Counties fall into one of four color-coded categories depending on the number of positive COVID-19 cases per 100,000 residents, and the percentage of tests that come back positive,” Newsom said. The four tiers, based on virus spread, range from widespread (purple), substantial (red), moderate (orange), and minimal (yellow). Alameda County is in the most restrictive, widespread “purple” tier. The county has 10.6 new COVID-19 positive cases per 100,000 residents, and a 5.6 percent positivity rate. Schools in the widespread tier aren’t permitted to reopen for in-person instruction, unless they receive a waiver from their local health department. As of August 31, counties in the widespread tier have been given clearance to open some businesses and activities with modifications. This includes all retail business, shopping centers, indoor hair salons and indoor barbershops subject to maximum capacity of 25 percent capacity. Alameda County Public Health Department however released a revised health order that limits hair salons and barber shops to open outdoor only. Gov. Newsom said that despite the roll out of this new model, individual counties can move slower than state guidelines allow. For example, both San Francisco California Governor Gavin Newsom and Napa counties were given the green light to reopen businesses indoors at 25 percent capacity. Napa County will move forward with the allowance, but San Francisco County has made no plans to loosen restrictions. They are the only two counties in the Bay Area with a less restrictive classification under the new reopening plan. The model also sets in place plans to reopen the majority of non-essential businesses. To move forward in the reopening

articles.text: The Common English Bible Study Bible informs us that “Philemon is Paul’s shortest letter, containing only 335 words in the Greek text. It was probably his last. Paul wrote it to prominent members of a house church in Asia Minor in the mid-1st century CE – Philemon, Apphia, Archipus and others. He addressed Philemon in particular because Paul’s concern was really about Philemon’s treatment of Onesimus, whom Philemon had enslaved. Paul wanted a safe welcome for Onesimus when Onesimus returned home.” Scholars warn us against reading Philemon through the lens of chattel slavery as practiced in the United States. However, since white Christianity has so studiously avoided reading our history, let alone the Bible through that lens, maybe we are well-advised to over-correct in regard to our interpretation and understanding of the perplexing book. articles.text: Campaigning during a pandemic is really tough. Candidates should not shake hands or throw campaign kickoff parties. Is meeting a masked candidate on a street corner or your front door appealing? You can’t tell what their face looks like. Lawn signs would not be fair to less well-known candidates, and I recommend we collectively abstain from using them, What’s left for voters to decide amongst the candidates? Endorsements from friends or prominent individuals? Perhaps a best practice might be to look at the actual job description of a school board member and measure candidates for that job. The California School Board Association created a white paper on the duties and responsibilities of a school board member. They are summarized below. School Board Duties and Responsibilities • Ensure the school district is responsive to the values, beliefs, and priorities of their communities. • • • Helping establish a long-term vision as to what students need in order to achieve their highest potential. Employing a superintendent and setting policy for hiring other personnel (e.g. teachers). articles.text: Editor: Every Piedmont homeowner knows the city actively ensures all building, rebuilding, and remodeling are at a certain level. So this city has ample precedent in ensuring every home is safe, the city remains beautiful, and the overall house stock quality is high. The Reach Codes are just the next step. Good energy performance (efficiency and solar) will continue to grow as a fundamental aspect of home quality. It would be decidedly retrograde, in my opinion, to think the measures in the Reach Code go too far or are simply not an appropriate focus for city codes. They are a logical next step, and a necessary next step, to sustain Piedmont as a beautiful and As the world addresses the crisis of climate change, let’s get on the –Jonathan Becker
articles.title: City Council should adopt the Reach Codes

articles.text: Editor: I met Veronica Thigpen last Thanksgiving. She adopted our family at the last minute when our plans fell through, and included us at her already full table. I was immediately impressed with Veronica’s easy-going nature, her intellect, and humor. One month earlier she and her daughter hosted young black girls from Piedmont for an afternoon social. Veronica engineered the gathering to help our girls find support in this homogeneous community. As a newer Piedmont resident, she jumped into action with a constructive solution to address the isolation our daughters’ experience in this community. Since then, I have watched Veronica exercise the same resourcefulness in all of her engagements. I know she will bring the same resolve to her role as a school board member. More importantly, I believe she will provide the kind of perspective the Piedmont School Board needs. When my daughters started elementary school in Piedmont there were more black children in attendance. By high school many of these kids chose to leave the Piedmont school system. I think we have to ask ourselves why? livable city. right side.
articles.title: Why I am voting for Veronica Thigpen for School Board

articles.text: Editor: Cory Smegal and Jen Cavenaugh are both running for re-election: Smegal for School Board and Cavenaugh for City Council. During my eight years on the School Board, I’ve had the privilege of working with many people. I’ve seen what it takes to be an effective board member, to work through unexpected challenges, to bring people together, and to move a vision forward. Cory and Jen are each extraordinary in their own ways, and they share many qualities that make them exceptional leaders: They listen. They question. They advocate. They are not afraid to say what they think. They prioritize collaboration and communication. They take leadership seriously.
articles.title: Urging the re- election of Smegal and Cavenaugh

Her ongoing concern of addressing Piedmont’s aging infrastructure will be much needed as we move forward. Yet she seeks to balance our growing needs with a realistic view of ever increasing fiscal demands placed on Piedmont residents. I know Jen is also aware and concerned about the significant retired segment of our populaSee Letters on Page 29 What exactly is the job of a school board member? By Hari Titan, Ph.D. Campaigning during a pandemic is really tough. Candidates should not shake hands or throw campaign kickoff parties. Is meeting a masked candidate on a street corner or your front door appealing? You can’t tell what their face looks like. Lawn signs would not be fair to less well-known candidates, and I recommend we collectively abstain from using them, What’s left for voters to decide amongst the candidates? Endorsements from friends or prominent individuals? Perhaps a best practice might be to look at the actual job description of a school board member and measure candidates for that job. The California School Board Association created a white paper on the duties and responsibilities of a school board member. They are summarized below. School Board Duties and Responsibilities • Ensure the school district is responsive to the values, beliefs, and priorities of their communities. • • • Helping establish a long-term vision as to what students need in order to achieve their highest potential. Employing a superintendent and setting policy for hiring other personnel (e.g. teachers). Overseeing the development, revision, and adoption of • • • • • • • • • • • bylaws and policies for the school district. Setting a direction for and approving the adoption of the curriculum. Establishing budget priorities, adopting the budget and LCAP, and overseeing facilities issues. Providing direction for and adopting collective bargaining agreements and monitoring progress. Acting with a professional demeanor that models the district/county BOE beliefs and vision. Making decisions and providing resources that support mutually agreed upon priorities and goals. Ensuring a positive personnel climate exists. Being knowledgeable enough about district/county educational efforts to explain them to the public. Evaluating the superintendent and setting policy for the evaluation of other personnel. Serving as a judicial and appeals body. Monitoring student achievement and program effectiveness and requiring program changes if indicated. Monitoring and adjusting district finances. I went one step further to create a nomination form based on these duties and responsibilities which can be found on my website, HariTitan.com. In consideration of this pandemic and distance learning, we might need additional criteria to consider. articles.text: I no longer have children in Piedmont schools, but I strongly believe that “distance learning” (virtual classes) is necessary until our county, state, and country gets COVID under control. Piedmont has been fortunate with only a small number of cases, yet the free flow of people from higher-rate areas enables the free flow of virus, and the numbers have been rising in Piedmont as well. Agglomerations of people in closed areas like classrooms is a sure way to spread the contagion to other students, staff, and to the people they live with. While in-person learning is clearly superior to distance learning, and necessary for the socialization of our next generation, the risk of spreading the virus, and the eventual cost, is a greater danger. How careful can PUSD’s students and staff be? I don’t believe that all students would keep their masks on all the time. Masks get stuffy. I get tired rebreathing exhaled CO2, and every once in a while I take off my mask to get a breath of fresh air. I’m sure kids are even less disciplined. I see them congregating in groups with their friends and everyone is mask-off. “Parental choice” seems to be an illusion. If there is no virus threat, there should be in-person learning. But so long as Piedmont and Alameda County are on the State Watchlist, there should not be in-person learning. How significant and reliable is the Watchlist? Many communities were off the list and now they are back on it. If Alameda County goes off the list, but adjacent counties are still on the list, are we really safe? A family might visit friends in Contra Costa who unbeknownst to them have the virus. Then the kids spread it in their classroom, and then into the Piedmont community. In-person classes are potential spreading sources. The Watchlist is an insufficient indicator; it is too temporal and too local. Parental “choice” is not an objective indicator of health safety; it is a personal willingness to accept risk. But the negative impacts of such risk could apply to people beyond a parent’s own children.

pages.text: 4 Wednesday, September 2, 2020 REACH Codes: Good intentions, unintended consequences By Carter Dunlap The REACH Code proposals are well intentioned and necessary in order to make progress with the City’s 2018 Climate Action Plan. No one opposes a cleaner environment. However, California’s woefully lacking electricity infrastructure makes these proposals aggressive and ultimately fraught with risk for Piedmont residents. A few years ago, a similar proposal relied on property sales as the triggering mandate for costly efficiency investments. The logic was that the costs would be borne by the buyer, presumably a newcomer. Having met with no success, the current plan rests on the assumption that homeowners wishing to do anything beyond very basic maintenance will be willing to incur the burden of these unrelated costs. The Reach proposal’s end goal is an all-electric, heavily solar powered Piedmont. However, advancing these goals could leave Piedmont more vulnerable and worse off. First, California’s electrical grid is far behind the ongoing demands placed on it. Its vulnerabilities have been experienced as recently as last week’s rolling blackouts. The state’s grid is more frail than at any time in the last 20 years. Impossible to ignore, the California Independent System Operator now has formally implemented rolling blackouts in the normal course of managing peak demand. Advancing these goals could leave Piedmont more vulnerable and worse off. Second, the growth of residential roof-top solar has provided a much needed and substantial addition to the State’s electricity supply, but with an accompanying volatility. Under the wrong conditions (low light, overcast, scant storage) the loss of solar at peak times merely exacerbates the peak demands on the state’s grid – adding further stress. As solar photovoltaic cost performance has outrun battery efficiency gains, most homeowners have found the investment in battery storage to not make sense. If the Reach Code program shifts the City to be even more dependent on electric and solar power, we will soon be even far more dependent on California’s aging, less reliable energy source, and undoubtedly more expensive than we enjoy today. When California is in a position to offer an adequate electric infrastructure at a reasonable Local Items cost, migrating our city to rely on that will make great sense. Until then, pushing Piedmont to be ever more dependent on that grid in hopes it catches up is foolhardy. Our homes will be more vulnerable to increasing uncertainty and rising operating costs. The City Council and residents should thoughtfully consider the next steps in reaching an important goal we have set for ourselves. articles.text: A private Instagram account was created in July by three Piedmont teenage girls as a safe place to anonymously share stories about sexual assault or misconduct by Piedmont High School students. By August 31, “Piedmont Protectors” had over 1,700 followers, and 101 posts had been shared about harassment, social pressuring, consent, and sexual assault, including rape. The posts caught the attention of Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, the parent of two PHS students. Before coming to Piedmont, he was assigned to San Jose PD’s sexual assault unit for three years. “As a police chief, I want to send a clear message to the survivors of sexual assault that I have heard them. I see the messages they have put out there and I take them very seriously,” he said. The posts on the account vary in severity, occurrence date, and content. Legal definitions of sexual assault, misconduct and rape differ from state to state. Wikipedia defines sexual misconduct as “any misconduct of a sexual nature that is of lesser offense than felony sexual assault.” Many students expressed relief at finally being able to tell their story. Some acknowledged blocking out past memories until given this opportunity. A few individuals posted apologies for their actions as well. On July 28 families of high school students received an e-mail from PHS Principal Adam Littlefield stating, “It has come to my attention that there have been recent social media posts involving current and former students reporting activity that is of concern. The school administration is aware of the social media posts that include information about sexual assault involving PHS students.” Partially in response to the non-specific nature of the message, the three students chose to offer immediate proactive support. A common narrative of the messages on Instagram involve juvenile males pressuring juvenile females to send nude pictures online, frequently through the app Snapchat. Tales of unwanted advances progressing into sexual assault predominate as well, with intoxication frequently involved. Bowers encourages victims of sexual assault to file a report. “They need to seek justice, and also receive the support of our partnered programs, Bay Area Women Against Rape (BAWAR) and CALICO.” A victim of any inappropriate sexual behavior can go directly to these organizations if desired. BAWAR was founded in 1971 as the first rape crisis center in the country. Visit www.bawar. org or call their hotline at (510) 845-7273. CALICO, www.calicocenter. org, has expertly trained forensic interviewers sensitive to the complexities involved. The Highland Sexual Assault Center (HSAC) has a hotline as well at 510-534-9290. These organizations can provide advocates to accompany victims during the filing of a police report, medical examinations and any legal proceeding. Questions about misconduct in any degree can be answered and counseling can be provided. Bowers has begun talks with Piedmont School District to find the most effective way to disseminate information to students and families on the process of reporting sexual assault. “Quite frankly, a lot of people just don’t know what’s out there,” said Bowers. “They don’t know they are entitled to an advocate through these interviews and investigative processes. They are not aware of the counseling services out there for them.” Bowers emphasized the importance of reporting the incidents. “[Reporting] helps to illuminate the individuals perpetrating these crimes. It lets them know that, number one, these things are crimes. If folks are left to continue to engage in that behavior described on the Instagram posts, how long are they going to be left to do that before somebody comes forward?” Chief Bowers also emphasized the role of parents. “Whether talking to their sons or daughters, parents need to have conversations at home about healthy, sexual relationships. I know it is uncomfortable, but these conversations need to happen,” he said. “If the conversations are not happening, kids are going to fill that void with misinformation from what they are seeing on the internet, and other people that may not be the best influencers.” A report can be made by phone at the Piedmont Police Department, tel. (510) 420-3000. Reports of sexual misconduct, harassment or bullying can also be sent anonymously to the High School through a Speak Up! form via https://bit.ly/highlanderhotline.
articles.title: Piedmont students lead response to sexual assaults

articles.text: Does your teenager want to explore his or her creative voice? Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir is offering a new online vocal music course for high school students. Called Future Voices: Foundations of Vocal Music, it will guide young people through a semester of training in vocal technique, rhythm and harmony, music literacy, and a special virtual choir project. The skills learned will support them in choir, musical theater, solo vocal lessons, and songwriting. No prior musical experience is required. The course will meet weekly on Tuesdays from 6:30-8:00 pm on Zoom, beginning next Tuesday, September 8. The semester runs from September 8 through January 9, 2021. PEBCC instructor Tim Silva is a skilled vocalist, singer-songwriter, and musicianship coach with a special gift for sparking creativity in young people. For details contact Silva at tsilva@piedmontchoirs.org. To sign up, contact registrar Anastasia Fegbeitel-Finn (afegbeitel-finn@piedmontchoirs.org). If there is sufficient interest, an AP Music Theory may be available. If interested, contact Artistic Director Eric Tuan at etuan@piedmontchoirs.org.

articles.text: Distance learning is challenging for everyone, but for students with learning disabilities this model poses increased challenges. Here are eight things you can do to help students with learning differences succeed in a distance learning environment. • Understand learning disability completely Understand as much as you can about your learning difference. Knowing the diagnosis— dyslexia, math disability, ADHD, executive functioning—is a great start, but maybe not enough. Find out what part of reading, math, attention, organizing present problems. • Reassess the Impact How your student’s learning disability affected them in the crowded, noisy, rigid, distracting physical school environment is different than how it will affect them now that they are in an isolated, silent and unstructured environment. Talk to your student, counselor, or neuropsych tester to reassess one’s needs. • Review accommodations Once you figure out how distance learning has and will impact your student’s learning differences, you may have to ask for new accommodations or figure out how the old accommodations will be delivered in this new paradigm. • Advocate in advance Don’t wait until problems crop up to advocate for new or more aggressive accommodations. pages.text: Wednesday, September 2, 2020 7 SchOOLs Piedmont students lead response to sexual assaults By Jay Russell A private Instagram account was created in July by three Piedmont teenage girls as a safe place to anonymously share stories about sexual assault or misconduct by Piedmont High School students. By August 31, “Piedmont Protectors” had over 1,700 followers, and 101 posts had been shared about harassment, social pressuring, consent, and sexual assault, including rape. The posts caught the attention of Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, the parent of two PHS students. Before coming to Piedmont, he was assigned to San Jose PD’s sexual assault unit for three years. “As a police chief, I want to send a clear message to the survivors of sexual assault that I have heard them. I see the messages they have put out there and I take them very seriously,” he said. The posts on the account vary in severity, occurrence date, and content. Legal definitions of sexual assault, misconduct and rape differ from state to state. Wikipedia defines sexual misconduct as “any misconduct of a sexual nature that is of lesser offense than felony sexual assault.” Many students expressed relief at finally being able to tell their story. Some acknowledged blocking out past memories until given this opportunity. A few individuals posted apologies for their actions as well. On July 28 families of high school students received an e-mail from PHS Principal Adam Littlefield stating, “It has come to my attention that there have been recent social media posts involving current and former students reporting activity that is of concern. The school administration is aware of the social media posts that include information about sexual assault involving PHS students.” Partially in response to the non-specific nature of the message, the three students chose to offer immediate proactive support. A common narrative of the messages on Instagram involve juvenile males pressuring juvenile females to send nude pictures online, frequently through the app Snapchat. Tales of unwanted advances progressing into sexual assault predominate as well, with intoxication frequently involved. Bowers encourages victims of sexual assault to file a report. “They need to seek justice, and also receive the support of our partnered programs, Bay Area Women Against Rape (BAWAR) and CALICO.” A victim of any inappropriate sexual behavior can go directly to these organizations if desired. BAWAR was founded in 1971 as the first rape crisis center in the country. Visit www.bawar. org or call their hotline at (510) 845-7273. CALICO, www.calicocenter. org, has expertly trained forensic interviewers sensitive to the complexities involved. The Highland Sexual Assault Center (HSAC) has a hotline as well at 510-534-9290. These organizations can provide advocates to accompany victims during the filing of a police report, medical examinations and any legal proceeding. Questions about misconduct in any degree can be answered and counseling can be provided. Bowers has begun talks with Piedmont School District to find the most effective way to disseminate information to students and families on the process of reporting sexual assault. “Quite frankly, a lot of people just don’t know what’s out there,” said Bowers. “They don’t know they are entitled to an advocate through these interviews and investigative processes. They are not aware of the counseling services out there for them.” Bowers emphasized the importance of reporting the incidents. “[Reporting] helps to illuminate the individuals perpetrating these crimes. It lets them know that, number one, these things are crimes. If folks are left to continue to engage in that behavior described on the Instagram posts, how long are they going to be left to do that before somebody comes forward?” Chief Bowers also emphasized the role of parents. “Whether talking to their sons or daughters, parents need to have conversations at home about healthy, sexual relationships. I know it is uncomfortable, but these conversations need to happen,” he said. “If the conversations are not happening, kids are going to fill that void with misinformation from what they are seeing on the internet, and other people that may not be the best influencers.” A report can be made by phone at the Piedmont Police Department, tel. (510) 420-3000. Reports of sexual misconduct, harassment or bullying can also be sent anonymously to the High School through a Speak Up! form via https://bit.ly/highlanderhotline. articles.text: The Piedmont School Board approved two tentative agreements related to COVID-19 safety at its meeting on August 26. One Memorandum of Understanding is with school employees (Classified employees - California School Employees Association), and the other with the teachers’ union (Association of Piedmont Teachers). The agreement with the classified employees is valid for the current distance learning format and in-person learning. The agreement with the APT is only for distance learning. “Anytime there is a significant impact on working conditions a new Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) must be approved,” Supt. Randy Booker told the board. Since many school employees, such as custodians and maintenance workers, cannot work remotely and are already on campus, this agreement applies to current conditions and future conditions when school resumes. The agreement with school employees applies to custodians, district drivers, maintenance, front office, tech support, groundskeepers, and administration. “This agreement represents a commitment to prioritize the health and safety of students and staff in order to minimize the risk of COVID-19 spread while also providing for the education of all students.,” the agreement states. Nearly half of the 12-page document outlines safety protocols. Notable points include a requirement for students and staff to check their temperature at home and stay home if over 100 degrees F. The district will be required to provide protective equipment to staff and students. Everyone entering campus must wash their hands upon arrival and wear a mask when entering, leaving and while on school grounds except for when eating or drinking. Protective barriers will be set up, along with hand washing/ sanitizing stations and hallways will be one-way when possible. The second half of the agreement addresses a policy for testing and tracing, accommodation for employees at “increased risk,” and a policy for requesting a leave of absence. The agreement remains in effect through the end of the current school year, June 30, 2021. A copy of the full agreement can be downloaded at: https://agendaonline.net/publ i c / M e e t i n g /A t t a c h m e n t s / DisplayAttachment.aspx?AttachmentID=1219630&IsArchive=0 results of which will be discussed at the next School Board meeting on September 9. The agreement states that the school district will not apply for an in-person learning waiver from Alameda County for students in TK through 6th grade until at least October 1. Dr. Nicholas Moss is Alameda County’s Director of Public Health Officer and is solely in charge of approving TK-6th grade waiver requests. Booker noted that Dr. Moss currently does not anticipate approving any waivers until after October 1 anyway. In California’s new color tier COVID ranking system, Alameda County is still in Tier-1 or “purple”, the most restrictive and the equivalent of still being on the state’s watchlist. After October 1, if Alameda County schools are eligible to reopen, it would be up to the School Board to apply for a waiver for TK through 6th grade in-person learning waiver. The district and teachers also agreed upon the new bell schedule which determines when each class period is to begin and end. Also agreed was a return to a traditional grading system and taking attendance within the first 5 minutes of each period. For the full text, download the PDF of the agreement at: https://agendaonline.net/ public/Meeting/Attachments/ DisplayAttachment.aspx?AttachmentID=1219631&IsArchive=0. articles.text: The Wellness Center Support Committee is pleased to announce the first annual Walk for Wellness, the largest yearly fundraiser for Piedmont School District’s Wellness Center. Walk for Wellness will take place September 21-27, and is an inclusive, accessible and socially-distanced event open to the entire Piedmont community. Event co-chairs KeriAnne Hohener and Nicki Gilbert expect that in future years Walk for Wellness will be a fundraiser that will bring the community together in person to celebrate the Wellness Center and advocate for student mental health. This year, participants will receive a Walk for Wellness visor and access to eight maps detailing various walks around town. “Families and small groups of friends should complete as many of the suggested walks as possible during the week of September 21. Everyone should post photos from their walks to @piedmontwellness on Instagram!” said Gilbert. “We hope to raise muchneeded funding for the Wellness Center while increasing awareness of the need for mental health services for our students,” Hohener added. The PUSD Wellness Center provides confidential, free on-campus and online counseling to all Piedmont High School, Millennium High School and Piedmont Middle School stuPhoto by Zak Gilbert Walk for Wellness co-chairs KeriAnne Hohener (left) and Nicki Gilbert display the banner for this year’s event. dents. The Wellness Center helps students manage common emotional and social challenges of middle and high school including stress, depression, grief, family or friendship conflicts, and substance use concerns. Approximately one third of high school and one quarter of middle school students receive counseling at the Wellness Center each year. The Wellness Center Support Committee is grateful to the nearly 30 Piedmont families who have sponsored Walk for Wellness so far, and to Bay Design & Build, The Cooper Group, Harmless Harvest, Mulberry’s Market, Niantic and Xantrion for their generous corporate sponsorship of Walk for Wellness. For event registration and donation information, visit www. piedmontwalkforwellness.org or email piedmontwalkforwellness@gmail.com.

articles.text: Alameda County is in most restricted Purple Tier in state’s new monitoring system Three new cases of COVID- 19 were reported in Piedmont in the past week, bringing the City’s total to 32. In Alameda County, the caseload was 18,445 as of yesterday, Tuesday, September 1, according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. This amounts to an increase of 1,707 week-over-week in the county, or a little over 10 percent. During the month of August, nine cases of COVID-19, the respiratory disease caused by the novel coronavirus, were reported among Piedmonters. Health officials reported 23 more deaths in the county since last Tuesday, August 25, bringing the total number of fatalities due to COVID-19 to 257. Oakland, the most populous city in the county, now has 7,448 cases. Hayward counted 2,612 cases and Fremont has 1,230. San Leandro reported 1,016. The rolling seven-day percentage of positive tests has trended downward through August in the county, with 5.2 percent of COVID-19 tests coming back positive in Alameda County. Alameda County was placed on a COVID-19 “watchlist” by the state on July 12, but now California is changing this system. On Friday, August 28, the state announced categories on a color-coded four-tier Blueprint for Safe Reopening. This new system went into effect on Monday, August 31. Alameda County is in the Purple Tier, along with 37 other counties in the state. This is the most restrictive tier, although it does allow for the opening of shopping malls at 25 percent capacity. articles.text: to hear their perspectives and support their efforts including PUSD School Board, Piedmont Connect, League of Women Voters, Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee, Parent Clubs, Piedmont Community Service Crew, Appreciating Diversity Film Series, Piedmont Parent Network, Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign, and others. 2 – Climate change is one of the biggest threats to our health and the environment. Evidence of the effects can be felt in countless ways, including the air we breathe today due to extreme wildfires and recurring droughts. Piedmont has made a commitment to do our part to reduce our greenhouse gas emissions, as 70% of emissions come from cities, according to Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan 2.0. As Piedmont is almost exclusively a residential city, we will need to work together to do our part in our homes and transportation choices. “In 2015, the three largest sources of GHG emissions in Piedmont were building electricity use, natural gas use for space and water heating, and petroleum-fueled personal vehicle use.“ We will have the greatest impact if we reduce our consumption, shift to 100% renewable energy sources, walk, bike and take public transportation or drive an electric car, and switch to electric appliances. Fortunately many residents embrace the plans and want to be a part of the solution because the city cannot achieve our 2030 goals through municipal changes alone. When the Reach code proposal was first presented to City Council, a few residents requested additional time to consider the proposal and some raised concerns that were not reflective of the proposed plan. I care deeply about community engagement and want Piedmonters to be informed and feel a part of the solution. Staff agreed to allow time for additional community education about the plan; thus, a Community Town Hall is scheduled for Thursday, September 3 at 6:00 p.m. The research staff conducted in Piedmont shows that most residents support the proposed changes. In reality, given the narrow scope of the changes, very few residents will be impacted. Staff built in options to allow for maximum flexibility, allow for exceptions for projects that would not trigger changes, and considered cost effectiveness with short payoff. I welcome further community input on Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan 2.0 and how we can best support the changes needed to reduce our carbon footprint. CONNIE HERRICK 1 – I am bi-racial. My mom was first generation Japanese and dad was a Scottish/Irish/English mix. There were 230 in my PHS class of 1975, and approximately 6% of us were of color. I know firsthand the importance of diversity and inclusion in Piedmont. My life experience as a person of color has taught me to listen well, seek out different perspectives, embrace new ideas and value open discourse. I embrace our differences. They make us strong. I am a 2-time breast cancer survivor. All of us who have faced cancer know this: you get an instant perspective on what is truly important in your life and your priorities become crystal clear. Two cancer experiences gave me grit, unwavering determination, perseverance, resiliency and an unending gratitude to be alive. Every moment is extremely precious to me and I am honored to offer some of those moments to serve our City. 2 – Yes, I support our Climate Action Plan and the Reach Codes. I encourage everyone to attend the September 3rd Reach Codes Town hall to understand how the Codes affect us, ask questions and voice concerns. These Codes were carefully developed with public input. There will be a menu of energy upgrades with many low-cost, easy-to-implement options. Replacing old, worn out gas reliant appliances, will only require completing a few of the easier, low-cost menu items. Only large scale building projects and new construction will require more costly options. Climate change directly affects all of us in Piedmont. We are living with higher temperatures, less rain and poorer air quality. Wildfires and floods are now an annual event. Through these Codes, we take the necessary incremental steps to increase our climate change resiliency. I encourage everyone to read our Climate Action Plan 2.0 and participate in the Piedmont Climate Challenge. CONNA MCCARTHY 1 – San Francisco in the 60’s and 70’s was the backdrop to my childhood. My father served on the SF Board of Supervisors 1964-68 and State Assembly 1968-80. Because our home was a constant source of political activity, I was exposed to “counterculture” ideals of peace, racial equality, gay rights and women’s liberation, as well as, equally passionate concerns expressed from folks advocating traditional mainstream viewpoints. Weekend outings with my Dad meant visits to residential neighborhoods where folks articulated genuine fear of losing The City they loved, to hippies, radicals and crime. We took urban hikes with Sierra Club leaders discussing CEQA, preserving Pt. Reyes, and the GGNRA. We investigated San Francisco businesses including a new rock and roll venue called: The Fillmore West. I learned first-hand the importance of affording citizens an opportunity to participate, that citizen involvement in decision-making builds trust, and, most importantly, that compromise is vital. 2 – Piedmont should help protect the earth’s climate through a unified approach to decreasing greenhouse gas emissions. Although early efforts for public outreach included 5 public meetings and 2 surveys, it is now apparent, as greater public attention focuses on this topic, bigger conversations are required. Our City Council did the right thing

articles.text: In advance of the November 3 municipal election, City Council candidates were asked two questions: 1) What qualities or experiences set you apart from other candidates? 2) Do you support the city’s current reach code proposal? Why or why not? The Post will ask each candidate two questions every week. Responses are listed below. JEN CAVENAUGH, Incumbent 1 – I earned an MBA from the University of Chicago and a BS from the University of Illinois. As a business professional, I had strategic and financial responsibility for large consumer products businesses and was an IT management consultant. As a Council Member for the past four years, I have made it my priority to balance fiscal responsibility with a commitment to improving Piedmont’s aging infrastructure and enhancing public services. I leverage my deep community connections to engage and promote diverse perspectives, develop mutually beneficial solutions, and increase equity and inclusiveness. I am actively involved with many community organizations

When equity is a core value, it requires that we examine what is being taught, whose point of view is represented and whose voices are missing. As the Zimbabwean proverb says, “Until the lion tells his story, the hunter will always be the hero.” HILARY COOPER 1 – I am in a unique position because I can represent three different groups of our community. I am a parent and volunteer, a teacher and an empty nester. I have a proven track record of raising money for our schools by co-chairing Spring Fling, The Giving Campaign and Measures G&H. Those fundraisers and parcel taxes have brought in over $10 million annually for our schools. I have worked in the classrooms at PHS as a substitute teacher and understand the incredible work that our teachers do on a daily basis. Now, as a community member, I serve on the board of The Cancer League and am a provisional member of the Piedmont Garden Club. Being a part of these three important cohorts lends me the ability to understand each perspective and help us all work collaboratively to ensure an excellent educational experience for all students. 2 – I think AB 331 is a good start to teaching the diverse cultural backgrounds of the people of this country. Some of our community may not be aware, but our district is one of the few to currently offer an ethnic studies course at our high school. The course is an elective, and AB 331 calls for the course to be a requirement, so our course will have to change accordingly. Beyond this bill and course, I would like to see ethnic studies material incorporated into the Piedmont curriculum in a broader way, with a focus on inclusiveness. We have a responsibility in Piedmont to teach our children to be thoughtful, compassionate and anti-racist leaders and citizens. As a school board member, I would look forward to working with the district and the community to continue to improve how we teach ethnic studies. JASON KELLEY 1 – As a parent who is currently supervising distance learning for four students in Piedmont schools—my girls in 6th and 9th grades, and my nephews for whom I am educational guardian in TK and 10th – I understand the challenges for students and families at all three school levels. I am in daily contact with teachers and other parents, and I see what is working and what is not as the year progresses. The community is grateful to residents who stay involved with the schools after their children have graduated, but I also think it is imperative that the Board of Education include parents who have children in the schools now and throughout their fouryear terms in office, otherwise that immediate connection can be lost. 2 – We should always be judicious when considering whether to add new high school course requirements, because we need to ensure students have room in their schedules to explore subjects of interest to them that can open up a wide variety of career paths. That said, I do believe that the course proposed in AB 331 would be a beneficial addition to the curriculum. The California Department of Education has shown that properly designed and taught ethnic studies courses lead to increases in civic engagement and community responsiveness for all students. A model curriculum that has been drawn up by the state focuses on four specific groups, and I would like to see local districts be able to expand on that framework in order to include additional populations they serve. HARI TITAN 1 – I am one of four candidates who have kids in the school district currently and one of three candidates who will have children for the duration of the 4-year term in office. Having kids in the district is especially important during a modified system of instruction and when board members not up for reelection no longer have kids in the school district. I am the only candidate who participated in school board debates since 2013. This is important for the continuity of institutional knowledge as well as a proven record of oversight. I initiated or expanded debates on deferred school bond property taxes, the cost-effectiveness of new high school theater construction over a renovation, improving STEM education, a net-zero STEAM building to reduce ongoing district expense, refinancing the 2013 school bond to save $26 million, and tracking and investigating declining PHS graduates going to prestigious STEM colleges, and school closures and reopening. My input was backed up with research, data analysis, and sometimes surveys designed to ensure all students, parents, and taxpayers benefit. 2 – Educating students about the diverse fabric of the American experience will definitely help reduce racism and bring us together as a nation. An earlier bill, AB 2016, required the district to develop a high school Ethnic Studies elective to be implemented by 2020. Piedmont High School’s Ethnic Studies course is UC A-G approved and was taught the first semester of the 2019-20 school year, a year before the deadline. I support the passage of AB 331 which allows any school district in California to locally decide whether to make this course a graduation requirement or not. Since the course is brand new, we don’t have dedicated funding just yet. Before making Ethnic Studies a graduation requirement in PUSD I would want to see how many students choose this elective voluntarily and hold hearings to get public feedback and discuss which graduation requirement it would replace. CORY SMEGAL, Incumbent 1 – As a School Board member for the last four years, I have important, relevant experience, I’ve made strong connections and I’ve shown that I am collaborative. During my term, the Board has faced a host of issues -- from challenging budgets to new curriculum to large construction projects. We’ve written and modified policies to improve the student experience. More recently, we’ve worked on student stress, teacher morale, and pandemic operations. Throughout this time, I’ve counted on the connections I’ve made. I’ve worked closely with every member of our administrative staff. I’ve built relationships with students, teachers, staff and parents at all levels to learn about their concerns. I’ve also worked closely with board members from other districts, sharing best practices. In all of my efforts, I am collaborative. I’ve learned during my term that Board members have to work as a team to solve complex problems. I think my experience is important and can strengthen the Board over the next four years. 2 – AB 331 would require completion of a semester course in ethnic studies for graduation beginning nine years from now. It just passed the legislature on Monday and is on the Governor’s desk. In 2019, the Board approved a semester-long ethnic studies course brought forward by an enthusiastic teacher at PHS. To quote the request, “PHS faculty have identified a need for students ... to develop a greater understanding of the experiences of people whose identity is not part of the dominant narrative in the United States... there is no opportunity in our current curriculum offerings where topics of identity and race are discussed in depth allowing students to compare historical narratives, social movements, and critical comparisons of various underrepresented racial groups.” I was thrilled to approve this course, which 27 students completed last year. It’s a vital addition to the course catalog and requiring this for graduation would be a good step. NANCY BOSTROM No reply received.

I initiated or expanded debates on deferred school bond property taxes, the cost-effectiveness of new high school theater construction over a renovation, improving STEM education, a net-zero STEAM building to reduce ongoing district expense, refinancing the 2013 school bond to save $26 million, and tracking and investigating declining PHS graduates going to prestigious STEM colleges, and school closures and reopening. My input was backed up with research, data analysis, and sometimes surveys designed to ensure all students, parents, and taxpayers benefit. 2 – Educating students about the diverse fabric of the American experience will definitely help reduce racism and bring us together as a nation. An earlier bill, AB 2016, required the district to develop a high school Ethnic Studies elective to be implemented by 2020. Piedmont High School’s Ethnic Studies course is UC A-G approved and was taught the first semester of the 2019-20 school year, a year before the deadline. I support the passage of AB 331 which allows any school district in California to locally decide whether to make this course a graduation requirement or not. Since the course is brand new, we don’t have dedicated funding just yet. Before making Ethnic Studies a graduation requirement in PUSD I would want to see how many students choose this elective voluntarily and hold hearings to get public feedback and discuss which graduation requirement it would replace. CORY SMEGAL, Incumbent 1 – As a School Board member for the last four years, I have important, relevant experience, I’ve made strong connections and I’ve shown that I am collaborative. During my term, the Board has faced a host of issues -- from challenging budgets to new curriculum to large construction projects. We’ve written and modified policies to improve the student experience. More recently, we’ve worked on student stress, teacher morale, and pandemic operations. Throughout this time, I’ve counted on the connections I’ve made. I’ve worked closely with every member of our administrative staff. I’ve built relationships with students, teachers, staff and parents at all levels to learn about their concerns. I’ve also worked closely with board members from other districts, sharing best practices. In all of my efforts, I am collaborative. I’ve learned during my term that Board members have to work as a team to solve complex problems. I think my experience is important and can strengthen the Board over the next four years. 2 – AB 331 would require completion of a semester course in ethnic studies for graduation beginning nine years from now. It just passed the legislature on Monday and is on the Governor’s desk. In 2019, the Board approved a semester-long ethnic studies course brought forward by an enthusiastic teacher at PHS. To quote the request, “PHS faculty have identified a need for students ... to develop a greater understanding of the experiences of people whose identity is not part of the dominant narrative in the United States... there is no opportunity in our current curriculum offerings where topics of identity and race are discussed in depth allowing students to compare historical narratives, social movements, and critical comparisons of various underrepresented racial groups.” I was thrilled to approve this course, which 27 students completed last year. It’s a vital addition to the course catalog and requiring this for graduation would be a good step. NANCY BOSTROM No reply received.

articles.text: Campaign to rebuild Piedmont Community Pool marked by weekend of work Kate Aubrecht, a swimmer with the Piedmont Swim Team, picks up fliers from Measure UU Campaign Co-Chair Anne Callahan. More than 100 volunteers with the organization Friends of the Piedmont Pool canvassed the city last weekend in support of Measure UU, the bond measure that would rebuild the city’s aged community pool. While maintaining a safe social distance, families, high school athletes, senior lap swimmers, and kids of all ages delivered fliers to doorsteps introducing Measure UU. The 56-year-old community pool is deteriorated and is facing permanent closure, leaving Piedmont families without a local pool. “It was really gratifying to see so many people come out this weekend,” said Anne Callahan, co-chair of the Measure UU campaign. “The current pool leaks 3000 gallons of water a day, the deck is disintegrating, and the city cannot keep sinking money into a facility that is literally crumbling. We must pass Measure UU, or Piedmont will be the only city in Alameda County that doesn’t have a pool for its schools and residents.” Members of the Piedmont Swim Team and Piedmont High School water polo team were out in full force delivering fliers up and down city’s hills. “A new pool would allow us to practice with our full team and allow members of our community to get their laps in as well without being impacted by our practice,” said PHS senior Max Wagener, a water polo player. “This is about more than just a pool, this The Krumins family volunteering with the Measure UU campaign: Adrienne, Esme, Peter (on the PHS water polo team, and Rik Krumins, and Holly, the dog. is about our community coming together to build something great,” he added. Longtime lap swimmers Valerie Villanueva and Paul Jahn volunteered last weekend to spread the word about the need to rebuild the Piedmont Pool. Duncan Watry distributes flyers in support of Measure UU. The Measure UU bond proposal would generate up to $19.5 million to replace the current three pools with a new facility featuring two pools – a warmer recreation pool for safe water play, swim lessons, therapeutic swim, and physical rehabilitation, and a wider, deeper competition pool for lap swimmers, high school water sports, and other recreation. The funds will also pay for new ADA compliant restrooms, a pool deck, and staff facilities that meet current building codes. “If Measure UU passes, there will be opportunity for further public input to shape the project’s design details,” according to a Measure UU press release on August 31. “Measure UU isn’t a choice between Piedmont’s old pool or a fancy new pool. They also expect a community pool.” When Valerie Villanueva was asked why she and her husband, Paul Jahn, spent the past weekend working for the pool, she answered, “The pool is one community treasure that really does benefit everyone. articles.text: Editor: I am writing to encourage Piedmont voters to vote for Measure UU on the November ballot. I grew up in Piedmont in the 1950s before the current Piedmont pool was built, and I had very limited access to a pool and swimming. As a result, I never became a very proficient swimmer and my enjoyment of swimming throughout my life has been limited. Measure UU will provide the necessary funds to construct a new community swimming facility that will serve Piedmont families, students, and seniors for the next 50 years. The current pool is at the end of its useful life. It loses hundreds of thousands of gallons of water annually from leaks and hundreds of thousands of tax dollars annually as we Band-Aid a decrepit facility. It must be closed or replaced. If voters do not approve the construction of a new pool, the current pool will be closed, and once again Piedmont’s children will not have a community facility to learn to swim and enjoy swimming’s benefits. This would be an unfortunate return to a period long ago when the city did not provide for one of the basic recreational and safety needs of its young people. I urge voters not to let this happen. –Dick Carter Dick Carter is a member of the Piedmont Recreation Commission.

articles.text: Editor: We strongly support Measure UU authorizing the City of Piedmont to sell bonds for a new community pool facility. Our family moved to California in 1978. We bought a house in Piedmont and then moved into an apartment hotel to wait for our furniture to arrive. It was summer and we all wanted to swim. Our realtor told us about the Piedmont Pool, and before we even moved into our new house, we bought an annual membership and spent most of the summer at the pool. Clive has been a lap swimmer ever since we arrived in Piedmont, so we have been pool supporters for 42 years. During those years our children, Margaret and Ted Chandler, and later our grandchildren, Megan and Genevieve Hiller, depended on the pool for swim lessons, a swim team experience, and junior life saving lessons. They enjoyed birthdays at the pool when they were young, PE classes at the pool when they were in middle school, and many end-ofschool parties. We all support having a place in town where every child can learn to swim and be safe around water. We have also enjoyed having a venue for the lap swimmer in the family. Now is the time for the City of Piedmont to build a new pool facility while they can sell bonds at exceptionally low interest rates. Don’t miss this opportunity. Vote yes on UU. –Clive and Ann Chandler Margaret and Jeff Hiller Megan and Genevieve Hiller

articles.text: Last weekend you may have received a flyer on your doorstep regarding “Yes on UU,” the official measure for a $19.5 million replacement of the Piedmont Pool. Nearly 50 Piedmont athletes took part in the campaign, as part of a group of more than 100 volunteers distributing fliers door to door to gain support. More planned outreach happening ahead of the November ballot. “We had about 45 student athletes help out. We’ll certainly have outreach by mail going forward. We’ll also have some student athletes calling individuals around town and doing more phone campaigning,” said campaign co-chair Anne Callahan. Callahan has some help with volunteer Patty Dunlap, both of whom mentioned how important a community pool at the center of town is. “It’s so important for growing kids to have easy access to the pool. They won’t have to depend on parents transporting them to other communities for daily practices. The more choices these kids have to participate, the more diverse of an experience they’ll have in their own town,” said Dunlap. Callahan, a Piedmont native, was on the PHS swim team when in high school. “It’s imperative, there’s no other way to describe it. I had my first job at the Piedmont Swim Club as a 15-year old and worked there through undergraduate and graduate school. It was a place where responsibilities and community input began,” she said. For sports at Piedmont High, adequate facilities have not deflected interested in pool sports like the swim team and boys’ and girls’ water polo programs. Boys’ water polo coach John Savage has reiterated time and again that kids are coming out for the boys’ and girls’ programs in record numbers each year. But to find adequate pool space, Savage has had to practice at Laney College, and occasionally to Concord. He said it costs each team $10,000 per year to practice at other venues and would be an eventual “death knell” to water polo if costs are increased. “It would be very difficult and expensive for the water polo teams to continue to operate. It would add strain onto the athletes and families with the greater commute and time spent on the activity. With our team growing every year, and the swim team and girls’ team doing the same, the demand is there for a new pool. We have been told by the high school that this year we need to come up with the funds for the pool rental. Asking for $10,000 per year is a challenge,” he said. For Savage the boys’ team has annually put together contending teams in the WACC and North Coast Section, pumping out collegiate athletes like Adam Low, Patrick Conn, and Henry Saunders in recent years. What the community hopes, is that improved facilities provided by a city-led public bond, will inspire young swimmers and young athletes everywhere in town.
articles.title: Student-athletes helping out with Yes on UU measure

articles.text: Photos courtesy of Associated Press Mackenzie McDonald played 21-year old Casper Ruud of Norway, who is ranked No. 37 in the ATP ladder. It was a long awaited U.S. Open for the tennis world after much of the 2020 schedule was wiped out due to COVID-19. Piedmont native Mackenzie McDonald returned to the courts as the underdog, and lost in five sets to No. 30 Casper Rudd, a 21-year old from Norway, 4-6, 4-6, 6-4, 6-3, 6-2. For McDonald, 25, the result was eerily similar to how he opened the year back in January’s Australian Open to Britain’s Dan Evans in another five-set loss where Mackie similarly won the first two sets and lost the final three when only needing to grab one more set to claim victory. And once again McDonald was seemingly on his way there after his opening 6-4, 6-4 victories, then getting ahead in the third set 4-3. But from then on, Rudd began dictating the pace with strong forehands to backcourt —keeping McDonald deep behind the baseline and unable to gain points at the net like he did in the first two sets. McDonald gained 13 points at the net by the end of the second set, but could only create nine through the final three sets. It would’ve been a monumental victory for McDonald after claiming two wins in the Western & Southern Open qualifiers the previous week. Since sustaining a hamstring injury and undergoing surgery, the tennis pro saw his ranking dip from No. 57 to 196 in February; it’s now at 243. Rudd entered with the No. 37 overall ranking. A win over the younger Norwegian would have set McDonald up with a favorable matchup in the second round against Finland’s 21-year old Emil Ruusuvuori, ranked No. 92. Women’s Ladder The talk of New York is the strength of the women’s ladder with some of the top-ranked superstars all competing with No. 1 Karolina Pliskova of the Czech Republic, No. 2 Sofia Kenin (who appeared in the Berkeley Pro Challenger in 2018), No. 3 Serena Williams, and No. 4 Naomi Osaka. Many are hoping to see an Osaka vs Williams rematch. The two have played three times, and the younger Osaka has won twice, once at the Miami open in 2018 and the other at the controversial U.S. Open Finals in 2018, where Williams’ dispute with the judge overshadowed the game. Photo courtesy of Tennis.com Naomi Osaka is among the headliners at this year’s US Open.

articles.text: San Mateo County still closed; a list of other park closed East Bay Regional Parks announced on Thursday, August 27 that it has officially re-opened all of its parks after briefly closing due to the smoky conditions produced by the wildfires surrounding the Bay Area. Six parks remain closed as they are directly impacted by the SCU complex fire: Del Valle, Mission Peak, Morgan Territory, Ohlone Wilderness, Round Valley, and Sunol Regional. East Bay Regional closed all of its parks on Friday, August 21 in response to this year’s extreme fire activity. Of the Santa Clara County’s parks impacted by the SCU fire, park officials announced on Monday Joseph Grant Park, Lexington Reservoir County Park, Harvey-Bear Ranch, Upper Stevens Creek Park, Sanborn Park, and Anderson Lake County Park remain closed. Santa Clara County also officially reopened Metcalf Motorcycle Park, Field Sports Park, Coyote Lake, and Stevens Creek Reservoir on Monday. In the North Bay with the waging LNU fire, the only closed parks within Marin County are the Point Reyes National Seashore, Tomales Bay State Park, Samuel P. Taylor State Park, John F. McInnis County Park, and Stafford Lake County Park. Marin County has an interactive map that shows if parks are closed or have other restrictions: https://zac-stanley.github.io/ MarinParkClosures_FullScreen/ In Sonoma County, the Armstrong Redwoods Natural Reserve remains in direct contact with the Walbridge section. Park officials announced on August 29 that they’ve begun reopening much of their regional parks. Only Guerneville River Park, Sunset Beach, Forestville River Access and Steelhead Beach remain closed. Some popular state beaches in Sonoma County have reopened like Sonoma Coast and Salt Point State Parks. Sonoma County is tracking their full list of park statuses at: https://parks. sonomacounty.ca.gov/ Visit/ Covid-19-Parks-Status-List/ All of San Mateo County’s parks remain closed due to the CZU fire in the Santa Cruz mountains and the Big Basin Redwoods State Park. Portions of the San Francisco Bay Trail and California Coastal Trail are open. The California Coastal Trail stretches 1,200 miles along the coastline from Oregon to Mexico, including 49 miles through San Mateo County. The parks surrounding Big Basin in the Mid-Peninsula Regional Open Space are now open. Only a handful of parks in the vicinity of the CZU Complex are still closed: Portola Redwoods State Park, Sanborn County Park, and Castle Rock State Park. As for Santa Cruz County, closed parks are: Wilder Ranch State Park, Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park, the Byrne-Milliron Forest, the Soquel Demonstration State Forest and upper portion of the Nisene Marks State Park. F R E N C H D O O R S T E P READ IT IN THE POST HIKING WITH JON East Bay Regional Parks reopen San Mateo County still closed; a list of other park closed By Jonathan Comeaux East Bay Regional Parks announced on Thursday, August 27 that it has officially re-opened all of its parks after briefly closing due to the smoky conditions produced by the wildfires surrounding the Bay Area. Six parks remain closed as they are directly impacted by the SCU complex fire: Del Valle, Mission Peak, Morgan Territory, Ohlone Wilderness, Round Valley, and Sunol Regional. East Bay Regional closed all of its parks on Friday, August 21 in response to this year’s extreme fire activity. Of the Santa Clara County’s parks impacted by the SCU fire, park officials announced on Monday Joseph Grant Park, Lexington Reservoir County Park, Harvey-Bear Ranch, Upper Stevens Creek Park, Sanborn Park, and Anderson Lake County Park remain closed. Santa Clara County also officially reopened Metcalf Motorcycle Park, Field Sports Park, Coyote Lake, and Stevens Creek Reservoir on Monday. In the North Bay with the waging LNU fire, the only closed parks within Marin County are the Point Reyes National Seashore, Tomales Bay State Park, Samuel P. Taylor State Park, John F. McInnis County Park, and Stafford Lake County Park. Marin County has an interactive map that shows if parks are closed or have other restrictions: https://zac-stanley.github.io/ MarinParkClosures_FullScreen/ In Sonoma County, the Armstrong Redwoods Natural Reserve remains in direct contact with the Walbridge section. Park officials announced on August 29 that they’ve begun reopening much of their regional parks. Only Guerneville River Park, Sunset Beach, Forestville River Access and Steelhead Beach remain closed. Some popular state beaches in Sonoma County have reopened like Sonoma Coast and Salt Point State Parks. Sonoma County is tracking their full list of park statuses at: https://parks. sonomacounty.ca.gov/ Visit/ Covid-19-Parks-Status-List/ All of San Mateo County’s parks remain closed due to the CZU fire in the Santa Cruz mountains and the Big Basin Redwoods State Park. Portions of the San Francisco Bay Trail and California Coastal Trail are open. The California Coastal Trail stretches 1,200 miles along the coastline from Oregon to Mexico, including 49 miles through San Mateo County. The parks surrounding Big Basin in the Mid-Peninsula Regional Open Space are now open. Only a handful of parks in the vicinity of the CZU Complex are still closed: Portola Redwoods State Park, Sanborn County Park, and Castle Rock State Park. As for Santa Cruz County, closed parks are: Wilder Ranch State Park, Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park, the Byrne-Milliron Forest, the Soquel Demonstration State Forest and upper portion of the Nisene Marks State Park. Campgrounds for Manresa, Sunset, and Seacliff state beaches are still closed. You can find a navigatable interactive map for Santa Cruz County at https://www.countyparkfriends.org/covidclosures. html.

articles.text: Photos courtesy of LeTour.FR Julian Alaphilippe holds the yellow jersey through Stage 4 after gaining the top spot in general classification in Stage 2. The 107th edition of the Tour de France is underway, the latest start ever due to COVID-19’s world impact. Through Stage 4, Frenchman Julian Alaphilippe leads, wearing the yellow jersey in general classification. For Alaphilippe, his ascent to the top spot is a bit of a triumph after leading last year’s tour at Stage 19. A landslide across the roadway and allowed Egan Bernal to eventually take over the top spot. Alaphilippe made his way to the front by winning Stage 2’s 186-kilometer mountain course, placing 58th in Stage 3’s 198-km flat course, then finished No. 5 on Stage 4’s hilly course, a length of 161 km from Sisteron to Orcrerer-Merlette. Alaphillippe said he was hoping to win Stage 4, but he relinquished six seconds to No. 4 Tadej Pogacar, who many marked as a favorite this year. “I had the double goal to retain the yellow jersey and to win the stage. It would have been special to win a second stage. I have no regret because the team perfectly executed the plan. I gave it all and I’ve been beaten by someone stronger than me. Moreover, I’m happy with my shape even though it’s hard to compare with last year. We won’t be able to keep that rhythm for three weeks. Soon it won’t be up to us to control the race,” said Alaphilippe. Bernal, last year’s champion, was able to hang around the top-five in 2019 before his fortunate turn in Stage 19.Traiing by 17 seconds, he faces a trio of mountain courses from Stages 16-18. Looking ahead this week, Stage 5’s flat course likely won’t provide any headway for the top riders, unless something catastrophic happens – like a crash. Even then, the mostly downslope course will provide relatively even times. Stage 6 is classified as a hilly course from Le Teil to Mont Aigoual, but it is mostly flat until the final 17 km ascent. After a flat Stage 7, the mountain courses of Stages 8 and 9 could be where the climbers like Bernal or Pogacar make their move. Here is the current top 10: 1. Julian Alaphilippe (Quick Step) - 18:07:04 2. Adam Yates (Mitchelton-Scott) - +:04 3. Primoz Roglic (Jumbo-Visma) - +:07 4. Tadej Pogacar (Team Emirates) - +:11 5. Guillaume Martin (Cofidis) - +:13 6. Egan Bernal (INEOS) - +:17 7. Tom Dumoulin (Jumbo-Visma) - +:17 8. Esteban Chaves (Mitchelton-Scott) - +:17 9. Nairo Quintana (Arkea-Samsic) - +:17 10. Miguel Angel Lopez (Astana) - +:17 Last year’s champ, Egan Bernal, is in 6th place, back 17 seconds. England’s Adam Yates currently sits in second place four seconds back.

articles.text: A’s in first place; NFL getting started; International Soccer from other major professional sports. It was an historic day in sport when on Wednesday, August 26, the Milwaukee Bucks initiated the league’s first social protest against police brutality following the shooting of Jacob Blake in nearby Kenosha, Wisconsin – about 40 miles south of Milwaukee. The Bucks’ players announced that they were boycotting Wednesday’s game against the Orlando Magic in the quarterfinals of the NBA playoffs. Their decision to sit out the game spread to the other teams slated to play that day: the Lakers, Blazers, Rockets, and Thunder. It marked a first for the National Basketball Association. But it wasn’t the first time players protested a game. In 1961 five Celtics players and two from the St. Louis Hawks refused to play in a preseason contest after Hall of Famer Bill Russell and two teammates were refused service at their hotel because they were Black. The Bucks’ recent protest spread to other sports leagues, including the Giants and Dodgers postponing their game in Major League Baseball. The WNBA also postponed August 26-27’s games. MLB – the “Swingin’ A’s” in first Another solid year is building from the little club that could, the Oakland Athletics. It is in first place in the American League’s West Division with a 22-12 record and a 2-1/2 game lead over the Houston Astros. However, a positive test of COVID-19 within their clubhouse has officially postponed their games until Thursday, September 3. It has not been disclosed whether a player, coach, or staff member failed their screening. Regardless, the A’s are in the hunt for a high playoff seeding. They bolstered their lineup with two former All-Stars ahead of the trade deadline, acquiring pitcher Mike Minor and second baseman Tommy La Stella. The Giants have a 17-19 record but were not active with trades at the deadline. Starting pitcher Johnny Cueto was rumored to be a player on the move, but taking on his $21 million contract may be an impediment for interested teams Here is a rundown of updates NFL regular season starting Get your fantasy teams ready. Without a preseason, the NFL is back officially next week on Thursday, September 10, with an opening game featuring the Chiefs vs. Texans. Aside from repetitive screenings and protocols for players, coaches, and officials, the season will run as normal from September through the Super Bowl in February. If players or coaches test positive with COVID-19, they will be isolated and treated as if they are injured, going on a Non-Football Injury list, and opening up a roster spot until returning. The San Francisco 49ers play on Sunday, September 12 against NFC West foe Arizona Cardinals. The 49er players and coaches have reiterated this offseason their desire to reach Super Bowl again, and they clearly have the talent, depth, and play callers to do it. But in arguably the toughest division in the NFL, the 49ers’ Week 1 matchup will say a lot. Arizona’s offense is re-energized with receiver DeAndre Hopkins, quarterback Kyler Murray, and head coach Kliff Kingsbury. The Raiders – that new team in Las Vegas – travel to the Carolina Panthers for Week 1. Their first home game at Allegiant Stadium will be in Week 2. In another tough division, the AFC West, the Los Angeles Chargers has lost quarterback Philip Rivers, but their defense is by-far the division’s best. If the Raiders push for a wild card berth, they’ll have to do well against the Denver Broncos and L.A. International Soccer UEFA’s Nation’s League gets started for European national teams starting tomorrow, Thursday, September 3, the first of six group stage matches. Games on the second match day will be played September 6-8, and then national programs won’t meet again until October after proclubs get their 2020/2021 seasons started. For the United States Men’s National Team, the country’s situation revolving COVID-19 has forced them into a bubble compared to their European counterparts. Teams within CONCACAF in North and South America are not expected to play until October. USMNT manager Gregg Berhalter announced that they will try to schedule friendlies during the Fall months, but the men’s national team will not play any meaningful matches until June 2021’s World Cup qualifiers. One U.S. player made news on Monday when starting midfielder Weston McKennie, 22, signed a deal to play with Italian super club Juventus. Photo courtesy of SFGate.com Don’t call it a comeback. The A’s are back in first place of the AL West. Photo courtesy of NBC Bay Area The NFL returns soon, but without a pre-season. It will go straight into the regular season from training camp. The 49ers are in the hunt for another Super Bowl run.
